hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when you feel rattled, where do you usually go?
options: me too. this story goes somewhere else. down.
honest. watch where the buddha goes instead.
then your body already knows this one. listen.

steps.line: In Buddhist tradition, on the night of his awakening, Siddhartha sat beneath a great fig tree. He vowed not to rise until he understood.
Then came Mara, the tempter, with storms and a shadowy army, trying to drive him from his seat. Siddhartha did not move.
So Mara tried words. “This seat is mine. My army will speak for me. Who will speak for you?” Siddhartha was alone.

steps.q: No one is there to back him up. He reaches down and touches the earth. What do you guess happens?
o: Mara laughs, and his army charges
The earth itself speaks up for him
steps.why: In the old telling, the ground itself answers for him. Not a voice from the sky: the earth he is sitting on.

steps.line: He didn’t argue. He let his right hand slip down over his knee, and touched the earth with his fingertips.

steps.q: Why touch the earth, instead of arguing with Mara?
o: The earth had seen all his past good deeds
It showed he was giving up the seat
He wanted to look humble before the army
steps.why: In the old telling, the earth had watched his good deeds over many lifetimes, so it could be his witness. He didn’t need a crowd.

steps.line: As the old texts tell it, the earth roared: I am his witness. And Mara’s army scattered like leaves in the wind.
steps.label: as the old texts tell it

steps.line: By dawn the storm was gone, and Siddhartha had woken up. From then on he was called the Buddha, the one who is awake.

steps.q: In many tellings, the earth goddess herself answered. How did she scatter Mara’s army?
o: She split the ground beneath them
She raised a wall of mountains
She wrung a flood from her long hair
steps.why: In Thai, Cambodian and Burmese tellings, she wrings out all the water he had poured over lifetimes of giving, and the flood sweeps Mara’s army away.

steps.line: Today that hand reaches down in temples and homes all over the world. And your own feet are on the earth too, right now.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Mara’s name comes from an old root word. What does it mean?
steps.why: Mara comes from a root meaning to die. Many Buddhists see him less as a monster than as fear, craving and doubt inside us.

say: here’s what i love. in that moment, the buddha didn’t go up into his head. he went down, to the ground he was sitting on.

one of the oldest buddhist teachings on mindfulness starts right there, with the body: breathing, standing, walking, sitting. know what your body is doing while it’s doing it. your feet are always somewhere to land.

steps.q: You see a statue: the Buddha seated, left hand in his lap, right hand reaching down to the ground. What moment is it showing?
o: His first teaching, to five friends
His last day, lying on his side
The night he woke up, under the tree
steps.why: The earth-touching hand, bhumisparsha, points to this night: the challenge, the witness, the waking at dawn.

today.say: today, when you feel rattled, try the buddha’s move: feet flat on the floor, hands resting on your knees. feel the ground holding you up. come back down.
options: good. the earth is a patient witness.
lovely. that’s the whole seat, right there.

card.keepWhy: Come back down. The ground is your witness.
sources: Nidanakatha (the introduction to the Jataka commentary), Avidure-nidana: the Bodhisatta sits beneath the bodhi tree resolved not to rise; Mara comes on his elephant Girimekhala with his army; Mara claims the seat and his army bears witness for him; the Bodhisatta, having no living witness, draws his right hand from beneath his robe and touches the earth; the earth roars that it is his witness; Mara’s army flees; at dawn he attains awakening.
Lalitavistara, ch. 21: Mara’s assault and defeat; the earth bears witness.
Bhumisparsha mudra (earth-touching gesture): common in Buddha images of the awakening at Bodh Gaya.
Satipatthana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 10): mindfulness of the body, including breathing and the four postures.
check: Mara’s line “Who will speak for you?” paraphrases the Nidanakatha exchange about witnesses. Confirm.
“The earth roared: I am his witness” paraphrases the Nidanakatha; in many Southeast Asian tellings the earth goddess wrings water from her hair instead. Confirm the label “as the old texts tell it.”
In the Nidanakatha he speaks to the earth before touching it (it witnessed his giving as Vessantara); the lesson says only “he didn’t argue.” Confirm.
Painting ET6 shows a small Buddha statue on a home shelf with a flower; confirm it reads as respectful to Buddhists.
